findings.claim: "As of May 4, 2026 FedRAMP uses 'FedRAMP Certified' with impact classes: Class C = Moderate, Class D = High."
findings.problem: Per the deadline SSOT (aan-authority-deadlines.yml), 2026-05-04 is the date of the CR26 PUBLIC PREVIEW (source: fedramp.gov/2026-05-04-public-preview-consolidated-rules-2026); the Consolidated Rules were launched 2026-06-25 and do not become mandatory until 2027-01-01 (cr26-mandatory). Attributing adoption of the nomenclature to the preview date misstates when the terminology took effect.
findings.fix: Cite the CR26 launch (June 25, 2026) as the point the nomenclature entered use, or phrase as 'introduced in the May 4, 2026 CR26 public preview and launched June 25, 2026; mandatory January 1, 2027.'
findings.verified_fix: Attribute the nomenclature to the CR26 launch, not the preview date: 'Introduced in the May 4, 2026 CR26 public preview and launched with the Consolidated Rules on June 25, 2026; mandatory January 1, 2027.' Do not present May 4 as the date the terminology entered use.
findings.resolution_evidence: Per aan-authority-deadlines.yml, 2026-05-04 is the CR26 PUBLIC PREVIEW date (source cr26-validity-end URL /2026-05-04-public-preview-consolidated-rules-2026/); the Consolidated Rules launched 2026-06-25 (cr26-mandatory source URL) and are mandatory 2027-01-01. 'As of May 4, 2026 FedRAMP uses' conflates the preview with adoption.

Verify every status on the FedRAMP Marketplace at the time...'), and every status cell carries the actual Rev5 level in parentheses — e.g. 'Class C (Moderate) (2019)', 'Class C (Moderate) — ATO 2026-03-05'. The real, reproducible authorization level (Moderate) is stated in each cell, so this is a disclosed-convention/editorial choice, not a non-reproducible 'verified status' defect.

Every other ✅ row records a CSO (SailPoint FR2001938710A, InfoBlox FR2017257053, ThousandEyes FR2523656707). findings.claim: The standing-assignment enumeration script pipes a `foreach` statement into Format-Table (`foreach ($roleId in $privilegedRoles) { ... } | Format-Table -AutoSize`, line 188) and the $privilegedRoles array has a trailing comma after the Intune Administrator GUID (line 161).

findings.resolution_evidence: Line 166 opens `foreach ($roleId in $privilegedRoles) { ... }` and line 188 closes it with `} | Format-Table -AutoSize`; piping a foreach statement is a parse error. This book never mentions BOD 26-04 at all, five months before its timelines bind and one month before agency policies are due. A hostile ISSO checks the 14/28-day tiers against the BOD 22-01 text and rejects the authority column.
findings.fix: Re-attribute the exposure-based 14/28-day tiers to BOD 26-04 (citing the registry dates), keep BOD 22-01 as the catalog-due-date authority, and add a transition note that BOD 26-04 remediation timelines are in force 2026-12-07.
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 74 now states 'BOD 22-01 sets no internet-facing/internal split; the per-entry catalog due date applies regardless of network exposure' and names BOD 26-04 as the superseding risk-based model. SLA table rows 86-87 attribute the split to 'BOD 22-01 (KEV due date); SSA SLA tier' framed as SSA's own operational SLA. Corrected.

findings.claim: Closure table row: "RA-5(5) | Privileged Access for Scanning" (repeated in fig-alt at line 1087).
findings.problem: The SSOT catalog (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json, v5.2.0) gives RA-5(5) the title "Privileged Access". "Privileged Access for Scanning" is not the official title; a 3PAO checking control titles against the catalog flags it.
findings.fix: Change the title to "Privileged Access" in the table row and the vuln-fig-04 fig-alt (and regenerate the figure if it renders the wrong title).
findings.resolution_evidence: Closure row (line 1099) now reads 'RA-5(5) | Privileged Access' and fig-alt (line 1108) lists 'Privileged Access'. Matches NIST catalog RA-5(5) = 'Privileged Access'. 'Privileged Access for Scanning' no longer present.

findings.claim: "SQL Server 2019 mainstream support ends July 2024 (extended security updates available through 2029 via Arc enrollment). SQL Server 2022 mainstream support runs through January 2028." (repeated in the vuln-fig-06 fig-alt, line 695).
findings.problem: Contradicts the same document's own CU map 40 lines later, which records SQL 2019 EOS as 2030-01-08 (line 734). July 2024 is the SQL Server 2014 date in that same map (2024-07-09, line 737) — the sentence conflates 2014's lifecycle with 2019's, and "ESU through 2029" matches neither. An assessor reproducing either date from the script or from Microsoft's lifecycle page gets a different answer than the prose.
findings.fix: Correct the prose (and fig-alt/figure) to the actual SQL 2019 lifecycle consistent with the script's EOS map, and remove or re-source the "ESU through 2029 via Arc" claim.
findings.resolution_evidence: Prose (line 714) now says 'SQL Server 2019 runs through its end-of-support date of January 8, 2030 (mainstream support ended February 2025; extended security updates available via Arc enrollment)', consistent with the CU map EOS='2030-01-08' (line 755). fig-alt (716) matches. The July 2024 / ESU-2029 conflation is gone.

findings.claim: "A machine that is more than 30 days behind the required patch level is marked non-compliant, which triggers the Conditional Access enforcement gate."
findings.problem: The compliance-policy script that immediately follows (lines 606-652) contains no setting that implements a 30-day patch-currency test: the comment '# Patch currency: mark non-compliant if updates available for more than 30 days' sits above an empty validOperatingSystemBuildRanges array, and no other property in the posted windows10CompliancePolicy body evaluates patch age. The claimed enforcement mechanism — the CA block on stale machines — is asserted but not implemented by the artifact offered as its implementation.
findings.fix: Either add the actual mechanism (e.g., populate build ranges from the current patch baseline, or use the update-compliance signal the platform actually exposes) or downgrade the prose to say the policy enforces the listed health criteria and patch currency requires an additional mechanism.
findings.resolution_evidence: Prose (line 622) rewritten: 'Intune's windows10CompliancePolicy has no native days-behind field; patch currency is enforced by pinning osMinimumVersion/build ranges... The policy below leaves those version fields empty for the agency to populate.' Now honestly describes the mechanism rather than asserting the empty array implements it.

findings.claim: "PatchComplianceRate (FedRAMP 20x target is 95% or higher for High/Critical severity across a 30-day rolling window)" — repeated at line 1102 and in the vuln-fig-07 fig-alt (line 930) as "the FedRAMP 20x SI-2 target".
findings.problem: A specific numeric threshold is attributed to FedRAMP 20x with no source; no FedRAMP 20x KSI in the series' SSOTs defines a 95% patch-compliance-rate target. Presenting an invented threshold as the program's requirement is exactly what a hostile reviewer rejects — and it creates a false pass/fail line the agency could be held to.
findings.fix: Restate 95% as the agency's internal target chosen to demonstrate SI-2 KSI performance, or cite the actual FedRAMP 20x KSI definition if one exists; remove "FedRAMP 20x target is" phrasing everywhere including the figure.
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 976 now: 'the program's operational target is 95%... this is an SSA program target, not a published FedRAMP 20x threshold.' Line 1123 and fig-alt (951, 'SSA program SI-2 target') match. The 'FedRAMP 20x target is' attribution removed everywhere.

findings.claim: "SLABreachedKEV ... must be zero for BOD 22-01 compliance" (line 955; fig-alt line 930 calls it "the BOD 22-01 pass/fail").
findings.problem: The script computes KEV SLA due dates as dateAdded + 14/28 days and never uses the catalog dueDate field it downloads and parses (line 304), even though the doc states at line 252 that dueDate is "the CISA-assigned remediation deadline, which may differ from the ... standard timelines". SLABreachedKEV therefore does not measure compliance with the deadline CISA actually assigned: it can read 0 while catalog dueDates are breached, or flag breaches that don't exist.
findings.fix: Use the catalog dueDate when present (falling back to the computed window otherwise) as the SLA due date for KEV findings, and align the pass/fail prose with what is computed.
findings.verified_fix: Use the parsed catalog DueDate (set at line 304 but never read) as the SLA due date for KEV findings, falling back to dateAdded+window only when dueDate is absent; align the 'must be zero for BOD 22-01 compliance' prose (lines 976, 464) with what is computed.
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 252 states dueDate is 'the CISA-assigned remediation deadline, which may differ from the BOD 22-01 standard timelines.' The DueDate field is parsed at line 304 but SLA is computed from dateAdded+14/28 (lines 380-381); SLABreachedKEV therefore does not measure compliance with the deadline CISA actually assigned.

findings.claim: PatchComplianceRate is the SI-2 KSI "across the active finding population for Critical and High severity (P0 through P3)".
findings.problem: The script computes PatchComplianceRate as 1 − SLABreached/TotalFindings over ALL findings including P4-Medium and P5-Low (lines 428-430), not over P0-P3. The published metric cannot be reproduced from the stated definition; also P0/P1 are KEV tiers of any severity, so "Critical and High severity (P0 through P3)" is doubly wrong as a description of the population.
findings.fix: Either filter the rate computation to the P0-P3 population or describe the metric as computed across all active findings; fix the P0-P3 severity characterization.
findings.verified_fix: PatchComplianceRate is computed over ALL findings (lines 428-429: 1 - SLABreached/$findings.Count), not filtered to P0-P3. Either filter the computation to P0-P3 or describe it as 'across all active findings'. Also P0/P1 are KEV tiers of ANY severity, so 'Critical and High severity (P0 through P3)' mischaracterizes the population.
findings.resolution_evidence: Priority mapping (lines 361-368) shows P0/P1 = KEV (any severity), P2 = Critical, P3 = High, P4 = Medium, P5 = Low. The rate divides SLABreached by $findings.Count (all findings, including P4/P5). Same mischaracterization at line 976.

findings.claim: P2 Critical non-KEV = 15 days and P3 High non-KEV = 30 days with "Authority: NIST SP 800-40 R4" (also line 76: "CVSS 9.0 ... carries a 15-day SLA under the standard federal framework").
findings.problem: NIST SP 800-40 Rev 4 is deliberately non-prescriptive and defines no numeric remediation timelines; the 15-day-critical/30-day-high numbers resemble the CISA BOD 19-02 requirements for internet-accessible systems. Citing SP 800-40 R4 as the authority for specific day counts is a mis-citation an assessor will check.
findings.fix: Cite these tiers as agency policy informed by SP 800-40 R4's risk-based guidance (or cite BOD 19-02 where it actually applies), rather than presenting the day counts as SP 800-40 R4 requirements.
findings.verified_fix: SP 800-40 R4 is non-prescriptive and defines no numeric remediation timelines. Cite the Authority column as agency policy informed by SP 800-40 R4 (or BOD 19-02, where these day counts actually originate). PARTIALLY MITIGATED: the prose at lines 74 and 82 already hedges these as 'SSA operational SLA' / 'follow ... R4 guidance' and notes the counts trace to superseded BOD 19-02 -- but the table Authority column still names R4 as the authority for the specific 15/30-day counts, and line 76 still says '15-day SLA under the standard federal framework'.
findings.resolution_evidence: Table rows at lines 88-89 attribute the 15-day/30-day counts to 'NIST SP 800-40 R4'; R4 gives no numeric timelines. The 15-day-critical/30-day-high pattern is BOD 19-02's, which line 74 itself now acknowledges.

findings.claim: CU map EOS values: 2022 = '2028-01-11', 2019 = '2030-01-08', used uniformly for the WithinSupport/EOSBreached test (line 771).
findings.problem: The EOS field mixes lifecycle phases: 2028-01-11 is SQL 2022's mainstream-support end (extended support runs years later) while 2030-01-08 is SQL 2019's extended-support end. Under the script's single WithinSupport test, every SQL 2022 instance will be flagged "End-of-support breached — immediate upgrade planning" in January 2028 while still inside extended support, so the EOSBreached count in the evidence artifact is not a defensible number.
findings.fix: Pick one lifecycle semantic (extended-support end is the compliance-relevant one), populate all rows consistently, and rename the field/summary label to match.
findings.verified_fix: 2028-01-11 is SQL Server 2022's MAINSTREAM-support end; its extended-support end is 2033-01-11. Every other row (2019=2030-01-08, 2017=2027-10-12, 2016=2026-07-14, 2014=2024-07-09) uses the EXTENDED-support end. Populate 2022 with 2033-01-11 (extended-support end) so the single WithinSupport test at line 792 is lifecycle-consistent.
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 792: $isSupported = $cuInfo -and ([datetime]$cuInfo.EOS -gt Today); EOSBreached = -not $isSupported (line 805). As written every SQL 2022 instance is flagged 'End-of-support breached' in Jan 2028 while still in extended support until 2033, corrupting the EOSBreached evidence count.

findings.claim: Intune Windows Update for Business rings (and the windows10CompliancePolicy at line 611) are the patch-delivery and enforcement lane for the Arc-enrolled Windows Server estate, with "domain controllers, database servers" placed in the production ring (lines 490, 553).
findings.problem: Not judged true/false, but this is the load-bearing remediation mechanism of the book and its applicability to Windows Server SKUs needs vendor verification: WUfB deferral policies and Intune windows10 compliance policies are documented by Microsoft as client-OS (Windows 10/11) capabilities, and the doc's own "Remediation Beyond Windows" section names Azure Update Manager as the tool that rides the Arc channel. If WUfB/Intune does not manage Server SKUs, the DC/SQL-server population described has no delivery mechanism as written, and RA-5/SI-2 closure claims for the server estate fail.
findings.fix: Verify against current Microsoft documentation; if confirmed client-only, route Arc-enrolled Windows Server patching through Azure Update Manager (as already done for Linux) and scope the WUfB ring section to the Intune-joined Windows 10/11 population.

findings.claim: MDVM "uses the Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) channel that was installed during Arc enrollment" / "No additional agent installation" (also line 54), and Windows Server 2012 R2 coverage "via MMA fallback" (lines 120, 133).
findings.problem: Not judged true/false, but two vendor-architecture claims need verification: (a) Defender for Endpoint's modern unified server solution is documented as using its own MDE sensor rather than transporting vulnerability data over AMA, which would undercut the repeated "no additional agent" claim; (b) the Microsoft Monitoring Agent (MMA/Log Analytics agent) was retired by Microsoft in August 2024, well before this document's 2026-07-08 date, so prescribing MMA as the 2012 R2 channel is likely stale.
findings.fix: Verify the current MDE-on-Arc onboarding architecture and the post-MMA path for legacy OS coverage against Microsoft documentation, and restate the agent-channel claims accordingly.

findings.claim: "Arc enrollment on 2012 R2 provides Extended Security Updates (ESU) at no additional cost."
findings.problem: Not judged true/false, but Microsoft's published model bills Arc-delivered Windows Server 2012/R2 ESUs as a paid per-core monthly subscription (the no-cost ESU applies to workloads running in Azure). A cost claim in a roadmap document that procurement will rely on must be verified; if wrong, it misstates a budget line.
findings.fix: Verify against Microsoft's ESU licensing documentation and either correct to "ESU available through Arc (billed)" or cite the specific no-cost condition.

findings.claim: "No vulnerability scanner automatically flags KEV status ... not linked in standard scanner outputs."
findings.problem: Not judged true/false, but this absolute claim about the entire scanner market needs verification: current MDVM, Tenable, Qualys, and Rapid7 outputs all advertise CISA-KEV/exploited-in-the-wild flags. The claim motivates the custom cross-reference pipeline, so if overbroad it overstates the necessity argument (the pipeline is still justified by the SLA-assignment and evidence layers).
findings.fix: Soften to "KEV flags in scanner output vary by product and do not carry the BOD SLA assignment; this implementation performs the cross-reference explicitly so the SLA logic and evidence record are self-contained."

findings.claim: "The daily compliance summary JSON produced by the script above maps directly to the CDM Agency Dashboard vulnerability data schema."
findings.problem: "Maps directly" to a named federal schema is a verifiable-sounding claim with no schema citation, field mapping, or version reference anywhere in the document; the summary JSON is a custom structure defined in this book. An ISSO coordinating with the CDM team on the strength of this sentence would find no mapping to hand them.
findings.fix: Either include/refer to an actual field mapping to the CDM data-exchange requirement (the Multi-Cloud Evidence Fabric book per the spine owns telemetry-to-CDM), or soften to "is structured to support onward reporting into CDM; coordinate the field mapping with your CDM team."
findings.verified_fix: Soften to 'is structured to support onward reporting into CDM; coordinate the field mapping with your CDM team,' or add an actual field mapping. 'Maps directly' to a named federal schema is asserted with no schema citation, field mapping, or version.
findings.resolution_evidence: The summary JSON is a custom structure defined in this book (lines 424-430, 967-970); no CDM schema reference exists anywhere in the file. Soft/verifiable-sounding claim.

findings.claim: Cloud-native posture feeds "KSI-CM (Configuration Management)" — stated in prose (line 174), in the fig-alt (line 181, "Card one, KSI-CM: Configuration Management"), and in the CM-6 row of the authorities table (line 165, "KSI-CM, KSI-SVC").
findings.problem: No KSI-CM theme exists. The spine SSOT (aan-compliance-spine.yml line 288) maps this book's CM-6 to ksi: [KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC], and the in-repo CR26 theme registry (AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md) enumerates the FedRAMP 20x themes — KSI-CMT is 'Change Management'; there is no 'KSI-CM' and no 'Configuration Management' theme. The table claims to be 'generated from aan-compliance-spine.yml' yet diverges from it, so a 3PAO tracing the KSI id to the FedRAMP 20x definitions would find a nonexistent indicator theme.
findings.fix: Regenerate the authorities table from the spine (KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC) and rewrite the prose/fig-alt to name the real theme id and its official name (KSI-CMT — Change Management), or, if Configuration-Management semantics are intended, change the spine mapping deliberately — but the doc and spine must agree and the id must exist in CR26.
findings.resolution_evidence: CM-6 row (line 165) now 'KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC'; prose (174) 'KSI-CMT (Change Management...)'; fig-alt (181) 'Card one, KSI-CMT: Change Management'. Matches spine line 288 ksi: [KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC]. No bare KSI-CM remains.

findings.claim: Fig-alt for the KSI figure glosses KSI-MLA as "Monitoring, Logging and Alerting".
findings.problem: The in-repo CR26 registry (AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md lines 42-46, 74) gives the official theme name as "Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing". Misnaming an official FedRAMP 20x theme in a compliance book invites a credibility hit from a reviewer who checks it.
findings.fix: Change the fig-alt (and the source figure spec specs/Vol_III_Book_04.yaml line 574, which has the same error) to "Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing".
findings.verified_fix: Change to 'Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing' in the line-181 fig-alt. The source figure spec specs/Vol_III_Book_04.yaml has the same error twice: line 559 ('Monitoring, Logging & Alerting') and line 574 ('Monitoring, Logging and Alerting').
findings.resolution_evidence: CR26 registry (AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md lines 42-46, 74) gives KSI-MLA = 'Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing'. Books 06 (lines 829-831) and 07 (line 194) already use the correct title.

findings.claim: Defender for Cloud is 'a clean fit' as the Moderate default because it 'does multi-cloud CSPM/CWPP across AWS, GCP, and Azure' — while the estate is defined (lines 61-62) as 'AWS GovCloud, Azure, OCI, plus Kubernetes — AKS/EKS/OKE/OpenShift', and the CM-6 closure mechanism is 'misconfiguration detection across CSPs / every CSP'.
findings.problem: The recommended Moderate default's stated coverage (AWS, GCP, Azure) does not include OCI, which the same document names as part of the estate; GCP, which it does cover, is not in the estate. The doc never says how CM-6 'across every CSP' is closed for OCI/OKE if Defender for Cloud is chosen — a hostile ISSO will ask exactly this, since the CM-6 row claims closure across CSPs.
findings.fix: Either state the OCI posture path explicitly (native OCI Cloud Guard feed into the evidence fabric, or acknowledge OCI as a residual gap under the Defender option) or scope the Defender claim to the CSPs it actually covers and note the OCI decision in the flag list.
findings.verified_fix: State the OCI posture path explicitly (e.g., native OCI Cloud Guard feed into the evidence fabric) or acknowledge OCI as a residual gap under the Defender option. Defender for Cloud covers AWS/GCP/Azure but not OCI, which is named in the estate.
findings.resolution_evidence: Estate is defined at lines 61-62 as 'AWS GovCloud, Azure, OCI, plus Kubernetes -- AKS/EKS/OKE/OpenShift'; the CM-6 closure claims 'across every CSP'. Defender's stated coverage (AWS, GCP, Azure) excludes OCI/OKE and includes GCP (not in estate); the OCI closure path is never stated.

findings.claim: Cloud-control-plane and container-layer questions 'are where most real cloud incidents begin: misconfiguration, excessive entitlement, and exposure — not an unpatched kernel.'
findings.problem: An uncited majority claim ('most real cloud incidents') presented as fact. It is a widely repeated industry assertion, but with no source a reviewer can strike it, and the book's motivation leans on it.
findings.fix: Either cite an authoritative source (e.g., a Verizon DBIR / CISA advisory figure) in the References table, or soften to a defensible statement ('a dominant class of cloud incidents' / 'a persistent leading cause in incident reporting').
findings.verified_fix: Cite an authoritative source (Verizon DBIR / CISA advisory) or soften to a defensible statement ('a dominant class of cloud incidents'). Soft/uncited majority claim.
findings.resolution_evidence: Uncited 'most real cloud incidents' majority claim presented as fact; the book's motivation leans on it. No source in the References table.

findings.claim: 'Prisma Cloud is the most complete CNAPP' (line 97-98) and Prisma Cloud/Wiz 'are the most complete CNAPPs' (line 189).
findings.problem: Competitive superlative asserted as fact with no analyst citation or evaluation criteria. In a procurement-adjacent document this reads as pre-judging the market and would be challenged in formal review; it also sits oddly beside the document's own recommendation of Defender for Cloud.
findings.fix: Attribute it ('per the agency's market evaluation' / cite an analyst source in the References table) or soften to 'among the most feature-complete CNAPPs'.
findings.verified_fix: Attribute ('per the agency's market evaluation' / cite an analyst source) or soften to 'among the most feature-complete CNAPPs'. Repeated at line 189 ('Prisma Cloud and Wiz for Government are the most complete CNAPPs').
findings.resolution_evidence: Competitive superlative asserted as fact with no analyst citation; sits oddly beside the document's own recommendation of Defender for Cloud. Soft.

findings.claim: Microsoft Defender for Cloud 'does multi-cloud CSPM/CWPP across AWS, GCP, and Azure and is available within GCC at FedRAMP Moderate'.
findings.problem: Vendor capability + authorization-level claim that must be confirmed against the FedRAMP Marketplace and Microsoft's Government service-availability docs at procurement (the doc does add a 'Verify on the FedRAMP Marketplace' caveat at line 191). Note also 'within GCC' is M365-tenant terminology applied to an Azure service — a reviewer may flag the wording as conflating GCC with Azure Government/Azure Commercial scope.
findings.fix: Keep the marketplace-verification caveat; consider rewording 'within GCC' to the correct cloud environment (Azure commercial/Azure Government) once verified.

findings.claim: Prisma Cloud is 'FedRAMP High-only, as is Wiz for Government' (also lines 190, 205-206).
findings.problem: External authorization-status claims sourced only to vendor blog posts (References lines 205-206). Authorization levels change; the FedRAMP Marketplace, not vendor blogs, is the authoritative record. The doc's own 'Verify on the FedRAMP Marketplace at procurement' caveat (line 192) mitigates but the References table should point at the authoritative source too.
findings.fix: Add the FedRAMP Marketplace listing URLs alongside (or instead of) the vendor blog links in the References table.

findings.claim: CM-8 row of the 'Authorities Closed Here' table lists FedRAMP 20x KSI as 'KSI-CM'.
findings.problem: The spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml, book-patch-sysmgmt block) maps CM-8 to KSI-PIY, and 'KSI-CM' does not exist in the vendored FedRAMP CR26 catalog (valid themes are 3-letter: KSI-CMT, KSI-CNA, KSI-CED, KSI-IAM, KSI-INR, KSI-MLA, KSI-PIY, KSI-RPL, KSI-SVC, KSI-SCR). Running `render_authorities_table.py --book book-patch-sysmgmt` produces KSI-PIY. A 3PAO checking KSI ids against the CR26 catalog would reject an invented theme id.
findings.fix: Replace the inline table with the current renderer output (CM-8 -> KSI-PIY).
findings.resolution_evidence: CM-8 row (line 254) now shows KSI-PIY, matching spine (CM-8 book-patch-sysmgmt -> KSI-PIY, line 272). 'KSI-CM' gone.

findings.claim: CM-2 and CM-6 rows list FedRAMP 20x KSI as 'KSI-CM'.
findings.problem: The spine maps both CM-2 and CM-6 to KSI-CMT (Change Management). 'KSI-CM' is not a CR26 KSI theme. The committed partial authorities/authorities-book-patch-sysmgmt.md is correct (KSI-CMT); only this inline copy in the .qmd is wrong.
findings.fix: Re-paste the renderer output: CM-2 and CM-6 -> KSI-CMT.
findings.resolution_evidence: CM-2 (line 256) and CM-6 (line 257) rows both show KSI-CMT, matching spine (lines 270-271). 'KSI-CM' gone.

findings.claim: SI-2(3) is titled 'Time to Remediate / Benchmarks'.
findings.problem: The official title in reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json and in the spine is 'Time to Remediate Flaws and Benchmarks for Corrective Actions'. The table claims to be generated from the spine, so this truncated title contradicts both SSOTs.
findings.fix: Use the full official title as emitted by render_authorities_table.py.
findings.resolution_evidence: SI-2(3) row (line 260) now uses full title 'Time to Remediate Flaws and Benchmarks for Corrective Actions', matching NIST catalog and spine line 269. Truncated 'Time to Remediate / Benchmarks' gone.

findings.claim: Table header comment states 'generated from aan-compliance-spine.yml; do not hand-edit'.
findings.problem: The inline table diverges from the renderer output in 4 cells (three KSI ids, one control title) and omits the generated 'Closure-Necessity — alternate-path rebuttals' block for CM-8 and SI-2 that the renderer emits. The drift gate (`render_authorities_table.py --check authorities`) passes because it only validates the authorities/*.md partials, not this inline copy — so this drift is NOT covered by the existing gate.
findings.fix: Sync the inline block (table + rebuttal bullets) with `python render_authorities_table.py --book book-patch-sysmgmt`, and consider extending the --check gate to scan the qmd inline copies.
findings.resolution_evidence: Renderer output compared against qmd lines 253-260: identical. Grep for 'alternate-path rebuttals' across Book 03 and Book 07 qmd: no matches -- the omission is not Book-03-specific drift.

findings.claim: 'the CM family feeds KSI-CM (Configuration Management)' in the FedRAMP 20x KSI Alignment section.
findings.problem: No KSI-CM theme exists in the CR26 catalog and no CR26 theme is named 'Configuration Management'. Per the spine, CM-2/CM-6 feed KSI-CMT (Change Management) and CM-8 feeds KSI-PIY (Policy and Inventory). The section's central mapping statement is wrong on both the id and the name.
findings.fix: Rewrite: CM-2/CM-6 feed KSI-CMT (Change Management); CM-8 feeds KSI-PIY (Policy and Inventory).
findings.resolution_evidence: KSI alignment prose (lines 267-268) now reads 'CM-2 and CM-6 feed KSI-CMT (Change Management), and CM-8 feeds KSI-PIY (Policy and Inventory)'. The 'CM family feeds KSI-CM (Configuration Management)' statement is gone.

findings.claim: 'KSI-MLA (Monitoring, Logging, Alerting)'.
findings.problem: The CR26 catalog title for KSI-MLA is 'Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing' — Auditing, not Alerting. The id is right; the gloss misnames the indicator.
findings.fix: Change the parenthetical to 'Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing'.
findings.resolution_evidence: Grep for 'Monitoring, Logging' in Book 03 returns only line 267 with 'and Auditing' (matches CR26 reconciliation line 42, 74).

findings.claim: 'Every stack in the actuation matrix is a CSP service, so its gate is FedRAMP — verify each stack's authorization status on the FedRAMP Marketplace at procurement'.
findings.problem: The doc's own actuation matrix includes stacks that are not CSP services: vSphere Lifecycle Manager on on-premises VMware (the doc itself frames VMware as 'on-premises'), Red Hat Satellite/Ansible on customer infrastructure, and MECM/WSUS (legacy, on-prem). FedRAMP authorizes cloud services only; a Marketplace check is inapplicable to these rows. A hostile ISSO would reject the blanket Theme F gate statement as factually wrong for at least three rows of the matrix.
findings.fix: Scope the FedRAMP-Marketplace gate to cloud-delivered stacks (Azure Update Manager/Intune, AWS SSM, OCI OS Management Hub, SaaS-delivered Workspace ONE) and state that on-prem tooling (vLCM, Satellite, MECM/WSUS) is gated by the agency ATO boundary, not FedRAMP.
findings.resolution_evidence: Theme F section (lines 218-232) now scopes the Marketplace gate: 'Most stacks... are CSP services... so their gate is FedRAMP' then carves out 'customer-operated stacks — vSphere Lifecycle Manager on on-premises VMware, and Red Hat Satellite/Ansible... which carry no FedRAMP CSO' gated by DISA STIG/FIPS and the agency ATO boundary. Blanket claim removed.

findings.claim: 'The native stacks mapped here are each FedRAMP-authorized CSP capabilities' (Stack Selection Status callout), and the overlay option is described as 'an additional FedRAMP-authorized product in the boundary' (Tanium / BigFix / Ivanti).
findings.problem: Authorization status of Oracle OS Management Hub in OCI Government regions, Omnissa Workspace ONE, and Tanium/BigFix/Ivanti cannot be verified from in-repo SSOTs and is asserted as present-tense fact here, while the same callout and the Theme F section say verification on the FedRAMP Marketplace is still required — the flat claim and the pending-verification posture conflict.
findings.fix: Soften to conditional ('subject to Marketplace verification at procurement') or verify each product's Marketplace status externally before asserting.

findings.claim: Vendor capability claims: Ksplice 'applies kernel and user-space patches without a reboot'; OCI Autonomous DB 'self-patching'; Workspace ONE patching Windows, Linux, and macOS.
findings.problem: These are external vendor capability claims that cannot be confirmed from in-repo SSOTs. Vendor source links are present in the References table (per the series' vendor-sources convention), but the specific breadth claims (user-space Ksplice coverage; Workspace ONE as the Linux patch mechanism for on-prem VMware estates) should be checked against current vendor docs — Workspace ONE is now an Omnissa product and its Linux server-patching role is the weakest cell in the matrix.
findings.fix: Verify against the linked Oracle/Omnissa docs; if Workspace ONE does not cover Linux server patching, point that cell at Satellite/Ansible or Aria instead.

findings.claim: Artifact 3 says US-CERT/CISA notification is 'per OMB M-20-04 (72-hour reporting requirement for major incidents)'.

Free-invented KSI names in a 20x-alignment section are exactly what a 20x-literate reviewer would flag, especially given the series' own CR26 indicator-count discipline.
findings.fix: Map to the real KSI ids — encryption/key management under KSI-SVC, logging/audit under KSI-MLA, boundary under KSI-CNA — matching the spine's ksi vocabulary.
findings.verified_fix: These four are not FedRAMP 20x KSI categories. Map to the real KSI ids from the spine/CR26 vocabulary: encryption/key management -> KSI-SVC, logging/audit/non-repudiation -> KSI-MLA, boundary/DLP -> KSI-CNA. There is no 'Data Protection', 'Non-repudiation and Audit Integrity', or 'Boundary Protection' KSI theme.

findings.claim: 'The minimum federal standard for symmetric encryption keys is annual rotation.'
findings.problem: No federal instrument sets annual rotation as a minimum standard for symmetric keys; NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 (which the SC-12 row itself cites) gives recommended cryptoperiods (e.g., up to 2 years originator-usage for symmetric data-encryption keys) and leaves the period organization-defined under SC-12. Stating a nonexistent 'minimum federal standard' invites an easy challenge.
findings.fix: Rephrase as an organization-defined policy choice ('this architecture adopts a 12-month cryptoperiod, within SP 800-57 Part 1 recommendations').
findings.verified_fix: No federal instrument sets annual rotation as a minimum for symmetric keys. Rephrase as an organization-defined policy choice, e.g. 'this architecture adopts a 12-month cryptoperiod, within SP 800-57 Part 1 recommendations'.

findings.claim: "These artifacts satisfy the IA-2, IA-5, AU-2, AU-12, CA-7, and CM-8 KSI requirements under FedRAMP 20x."

findings.fix: Map the five evidence artifacts to actual KSI themes (e.g., KSI-IAM, KSI-MLA) per the spine's ksi field, and soften "satisfy" to "provide evidence toward."
findings.verified_fix: FedRAMP 20x KSIs are themed indicators (KSI-IAM, KSI-MLA, etc.), not keyed by NIST control id — there is no 'IA-2 KSI requirement.' Rewrite to map the artifacts to KSI themes and provide-evidence language, e.g. 'These artifacts provide KSI evidence (KSI-IAM for identity/authentication, KSI-MLA for monitoring/logging) toward the IA-2, IA-5, AU-2, AU-12, CA-7 and CM-8 control obligations.'
findings.resolution_evidence: Spine models KSIs as themes throughout the closures block (ksi: [KSI-IAM]/[KSI-MLA]/...); authority registry (spine line 79) describes fedramp-20x as 'CR26 Key Security Indicators.' CR26 = 46 themed indicators / 10 themes, not per-NIST-control requirements.

findings.claim: The Arc Managed Identity certificate "is not accessible to any user or process outside the agent context" (and line 102: "No human ever sees the certificate or its private key").

A hostile reviewer will demand the threat-model caveat; as written it reads as a security guarantee the vendor does not make.
findings.fix: Qualify: certificate is managed and rotated by the Arc agent and not exposed through any configuration surface; local-admin compromise of the host still compromises the identity (which is why host hardening and PAM controls in Vol III apply).
findings.resolution_evidence: Lines 102 ('No human ever sees the certificate or its private key') and 136 ('not accessible to any user or process outside the agent context') are accurate for normal operation of an Arc managed-identity cert. The requested change is a threat-model hardening caveat (local-admin/SYSTEM edge case) — an editorial refinement, not a factual error in the mechanism as described.

findings.claim: "Kerberos tickets expire at five minutes of clock skew."
findings.problem: Misstates the mechanism: tickets have their own lifetime (typically 10 hours); the 5-minute figure is the default maximum tolerable clock skew, beyond which authentication requests are rejected (KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW) — the ticket doesn't "expire."
findings.fix: Rephrase: "Kerberos rejects authentication when client/server clocks differ by more than the default five-minute skew tolerance."
findings.resolution_evidence: General-knowledge Kerberos nuance (5 min is the default clock-skew tolerance, ticket lifetime is separate ~10h). Not repo-SSOT-verifiable and directionally correct as a clock-sync requirement in a bullet titled 'Clock synchronization'; defensible simplification. Out of scope for a 'live' SSOT defect.

findings.claim: "NTLM logon events have LogonType = 3 and AuthenticationPackage = NTLM."
findings.problem: Over-specific as a discovery filter: LogonType 3 is simply "network logon" (Kerberos network logons are also type 3), and NTLM can appear under other logon types (2 interactive, 10 RemoteInteractive). Filtering on LogonType=3 AND Package=NTLM misses NTLM RDP/interactive events during Phase A discovery.
findings.fix: Filter on the Authentication Package field (NTLM / NtLmSsp) across all logon types; note that Kerberos vs NTLM is distinguished by the package field, not the logon type.
findings.resolution_evidence: Defensible in context: SQL Server connections are network logons (type 3), so the discovery filter is reasonable for the stated estate. General Windows-eventing nuance, not repo-SSOT-verifiable.

findings.claim: "a credential architecture designed in 1999. Kerberos was built for..."
findings.problem: Kerberos was designed at MIT in the late 1980s (Kerberos v5 standardized in RFC 1510, 1993); 1999 is roughly when Microsoft implemented it for Windows 2000. Minor, but a pedantic reviewer will note it.
findings.fix: Say "adopted by Windows in 1999/2000" or "designed in the late 1980s for campus LANs."
findings.resolution_evidence: Defensible framing: 'credential architecture designed in 1999' plausibly refers to the Windows AD / Windows 2000 credential architecture (1999-2000 era), not Kerberos' MIT origin. Pedantic, not repo-SSOT-verifiable.

findings.claim: "No action in Books 01–07 is irreversible. The first irreversible action is `DROP LOGIN` in Book 05"
findings.problem: The two sentences contradict each other in the same paragraph: Book 05 is inside the Books 01–07 range, and Book 05 Phase 4 (line ~410) does execute DROP LOGIN. A reviewer reading the safety model cannot tell which books are actually reversible.
findings.fix: Change to "No action in Books 01–04 is irreversible" (or restate: the first irreversible action is the Phase-4 DROP LOGIN in Book 05, gated behind the 30-day observation).
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 41 rewritten: 'Every action up to that point is reversible; the first irreversible action is DROP LOGIN in Book 05 — and that action is explicitly gated behind a 30-day observation period.' The self-contradictory 'No action in Books 01-07 is irreversible' phrasing is gone; text is now internally consistent.

findings.claim: NTLM source-identification script filters `$_.Properties[8].Value -eq 'NTLM'` with comment "AuthenticationPackageName", then in the same pipeline labels `Properties[8]` as "LogonType"
findings.problem: Internally contradictory and produces a false negative: Properties[8] cannot be both AuthenticationPackageName and LogonType. In event 4624, index 8 is LogonType (a number) and AuthenticationPackageName is index 10, so the filter matches nothing and the NTLM export is always empty — which then satisfies Book 03 closure condition 3 ("NTLM sources classified") with fabricated-clean evidence. A 3PAO testing the runbook would reject it.
findings.fix: Use the correct property index per event id (4624: LogonType=Properties[8], AuthenticationPackageName=Properties[10]) or filter on the event XML field name instead of positional index, and correct the Select-Object labels.
findings.resolution_evidence: Filter (line 229) now '$_.Properties[10].Value -eq "NTLM"  # AuthenticationPackageName (index 10 in event 4624; index 8 is LogonType)' and the Select-Object label (line 235) correctly maps LogonType to Properties[8]. The positional-index bug and false-negative are corrected.

findings.claim: Phase 2 validation: "Expected output: `Authentication scheme: KERBEROS` (for Entra ID token-based connections on the server side)"
findings.problem: Contradicts the document's own Book 09 doctrine, which argues token-based authentication is precisely NOT Kerberos ("Kerberos is session- and location-bound... the token-based authentication these runbooks deploy"). If Entra token connections reported KERBEROS, the Book 09 monitoring logic and the series' Kerberos-replacement argument would be incoherent; the actual auth_scheme value for Entra connections also needs external verification against Microsoft docs before an operator uses it as a pass/fail gate.
findings.fix: Verify the actual sys.dm_exec_connections auth_scheme value returned by Entra-authenticated connections on Arc-enabled SQL Server 2022 and state that value; do not tell operators to expect KERBEROS for a token-based connection.
findings.verified_fix: Do not tell operators to expect KERBEROS for a token-based (Entra) connection — it contradicts this guide's own Book 09 doctrine (line 671) that token auth is precisely NOT Kerberos, and the auth_scheme enum at line 136 treats KERBEROS as a distinct legacy scheme. Verify the real sys.dm_exec_connections.auth_scheme value returned by an Entra-authenticated connection on Arc-enabled SQL Server 2022 against Microsoft docs and state that value. (Line 490 repeats '# Expected: KERBEROS' — fix both.)
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 671 (Book 09): 'the token-based authentication these runbooks deploy is the only mechanism that closes IA-2'; the whole series argues token auth replaces Kerberos and NTLM-fallback detection keys on the scheme. If Entra token connections reported KERBEROS, the Book 03 audit (line 136 flags by scheme) and the Kerberos-replacement argument are incoherent. True auth_scheme value not SSOT-verifiable here — flag for MS-docs verification.

findings.claim: Zombie-instance utilization query: `CAST(ring_buffer_address AS XML)` and `sys.dm_os_ring_buffers.timestamp - cpu_tick_count`
findings.problem: The query cannot run as written: the XML payload of sys.dm_os_ring_buffers is the `record` column (ring_buffer_address is a varbinary memory address that fails CAST to XML), and `cpu_tick_count` is not a column in scope (the standard pattern joins sys.dm_os_sys_info ms_ticks). The RETIRE/CONSOLIDATE disposition evidence this feeds is therefore not reproducible from the runbook.
findings.fix: Rewrite using the documented pattern: CAST(record AS XML) and DATEADD(ms, rb.timestamp - si.ms_ticks, GETDATE()) joined to sys.dm_os_sys_info si.
findings.verified_fix: Query cannot run as written. sys.dm_os_ring_buffers exposes its XML payload in the `record` column (ring_buffer_address is a varbinary memory address that fails CAST to XML), and cpu_tick_count is not in scope. Use the documented pattern: CROSS APPLY (SELECT CAST(record AS XML) AS record), and DATEADD(ms, rb.timestamp - si.ms_ticks, GETDATE()) joined to sys.dm_os_sys_info si (ms_ticks).
findings.resolution_evidence: Lines 145-153. sys.dm_os_ring_buffers columns are ring_buffer_address (varbinary), ring_buffer_type, timestamp, record (nvarchar XML). CAST(ring_buffer_address AS XML) and bare cpu_tick_count are both invalid; the RETIRE/CONSOLIDATE disposition evidence this feeds is not reproducible.

findings.claim: "Testing against SQL Server 2019 with the Entra extension is acceptable for Books 03 and 04"
findings.problem: Book 04's own completion criteria include enabling Entra authentication via `ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET EXTERNAL AUTHENTICATION PROVIDER ENABLED`, which the file itself labels "For SQL Server 2022:" (line ~341) — Entra authentication for Arc-enabled SQL Server requires 2022. Book 04 cannot be meaningfully validated on 2019, contradicting the test-environment guidance.
findings.fix: Restrict the 2019 allowance to Book 03 (audit only), or state which Book 04 steps (Arc agent + extension install only, not Entra enablement) are testable on 2019.
findings.verified_fix: Restrict the 2019 allowance to Book 03 (audit only). Book 04 ('Arc Deployment and Managed Identity', section starting line 253) includes 'Enable Entra Authentication on SQL Server' via ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET EXTERNAL AUTHENTICATION PROVIDER ENABLED (line 343), which the file itself labels 'For SQL Server 2022:' (line 341) — so Book 04 cannot be validated on 2019. Reword to 'acceptable for Book 03; Book 04's Entra-enablement and Book 05 require 2022.'
findings.resolution_evidence: Book 04 header at line 253; its Entra-enable step (lines 341-343) is 2022-only. Line 43's allowance for Book 04 on 2019 is internally contradicted by Book 04's own 2022 requirement.

findings.claim: "the token-based authentication these runbooks deploy is the only mechanism that closes IA-2 for SQL Server on modern transport"
findings.problem: An exclusivity ("only mechanism that closes") closure-necessity claim with no spine backing: aan-compliance-spine.yml registers zero closures for book-08 (or its companion book-07), and the only IA-2 closure row in the spine belongs to book-sn-saas with necessity: false. Until an IA-2 closure row with a necessity flag and alternative_rebuttal exists for this book, a hostile ISSO reads this as an unregistered, unrebutted necessity assertion.
findings.fix: Either back-fill the IA-2 closure (with necessity + alternative_rebuttal) for this book in aan-compliance-spine.yml, or soften to "the mechanism this series uses to close IA-2 for SQL Server on multipath transport" until the spine row exists.
findings.resolution_evidence: The claim is scoped ('the only mechanism that closes IA-2 for SQL Server on modern transport') — narrower than, and not contradicted by, the spine's only IA-2 row (book-sn-saas, line 334), which is a different scope (SaaS SSO federation, necessity:false). Spine back-fill for book-08 is explicitly pending (spine line 17). This is an unregistered-but-defensible scoped doctrine statement, not a factual error.

findings.claim: "SQL Server 2019 instances have ESU coverage confirmed via Arc enrollment (free via Arc)"
findings.problem: Two Microsoft-lifecycle claims that need verification against Microsoft before an assessor relies on them: (a) whether SQL Server 2019 needs ESUs at all in 2026 (its extended support window is generally understood to run to 2030, making ESU inapplicable), and (b) whether ESUs delivered through Arc are free (Arc-delivered ESUs are generally a paid monthly subscription; the free-ESU benefit applies to Azure-hosted workloads). As written the checklist item may direct agencies to confirm a benefit that does not exist.
findings.fix: Verify against Microsoft lifecycle/Arc ESU documentation and either delete the ESU item for 2019 or restate which versions need ESU and the actual Arc ESU cost model.

findings.claim: Linked-server remediation: `sp_addlinkedsrvlogin ... @rmtuser = 'svc-linkedserver@agency.gov', @rmtpassword = NULL; -- Token authentication — no password`
findings.problem: The claim that passing an Entra UPN as @rmtuser with a NULL password yields token authentication needs verification against Microsoft documentation — sp_addlinkedsrvlogin's rmtuser/rmtpassword pair is the SQL-authentication mapping, and Entra-based linked-server authentication is normally configured through the OLE DB provider/connection options, not a NULL password. As written the runbook step may simply create a mapping that fails to authenticate.
findings.fix: Verify the supported Entra authentication path for linked servers on SQL Server 2022 and replace the snippet with the documented mechanism; remove the "Token authentication — no password" annotation if unsupported.

findings.claim: Conditional Access target: "Cloud app = Azure SQL (App ID 022907d3-0f1b-48f7-badc-1ba6abab6d66)"
findings.problem: A hard-coded first-party application GUID that an assessor will check; it also needs confirmation that Conditional Access policies scoped to the Azure SQL cloud app actually govern Entra token issuance for Arc-enabled SQL Server (not just Azure SQL Database/MI), and whether the same App ID applies in Azure Government (usgovvirginia is the region used elsewhere in this guide).
findings.fix: Verify the App ID and its applicability to Arc-enabled SQL Server in Azure Government against Microsoft documentation and cite the source.

findings.claim: Caption: "The five closure conditions gate progression from authentication audit to Arc deployment" on image figs/san-fig-03-ntlm-elimination.png
findings.problem: The caption claims the figure shows the five closure conditions, but the image file and its fig-alt ("Diagram showing NTLM elimination phases and source patterns") describe a different, reused diagram — the figure does not depict what the caption asserts.
findings.fix: Either author a five-closure-conditions figure or rewrite the caption/fig-alt to describe the NTLM-elimination diagram actually shown.
findings.verified_fix: Author a five-closure-conditions figure, or rewrite the caption and fig-alt to describe the NTLM-elimination diagram actually shown. The reused image file (san-fig-03-ntlm-elimination.png, same asset as Vol II Book 01 fig-san03) and its fig-alt depict NTLM elimination phases, not the five closure conditions the caption asserts.
findings.resolution_evidence: Caption claims 'five closure conditions' but points at figs/san-fig-03-ntlm-elimination.png with fig-alt 'Diagram showing NTLM elimination phases and source patterns' — the same file used for NTLM elimination in Book 01 line 142. Figure does not depict what the caption asserts.

findings.claim: "It closes the control families that are satisfied by artifacts rather than configuration: contingency planning (CP), supply-chain risk (SR), program management (PM), privacy/PII processing (PT), awareness and training (AT), and assessment/authorization/continuous monitoring (CA)."
findings.problem: The closure registry SSOT (aan-compliance-spine.yml) contains zero closure rows for any Vol IV book (book-14 through book-19), and no CP-, SR-, PM-, PT-, or AT-family closures anywhere in the file (the only CA closures belong to Vol III/VII books). The spine's own status note says closures are still being back-filled per book, so the volume-level 'closes' assertion cannot currently be reproduced from the SSOT — a 3PAO asking for the control-to-book closure mapping behind this sentence would find nothing registered.
findings.fix: Either soften to forward-looking language ('the volume's books carry the closures for CP/SR/PM/PT/AT/CA — registered per book in the compliance spine as each book is finalized'), or back-fill the spine closure rows for book-14..book-19 before shipping this overview.
findings.verified_fix: Soften to forward-looking: 'the volume's books carry the closures for CP/SR/PM/PT/AT/CA — registered per book in the compliance spine as each book is finalized.'
findings.resolution_evidence: aan-compliance-spine.yml closures: block has ZERO rows for book-14..book-19 (grep 'book: book-1[4-9]' returns nothing); only book-net-enforce/patch/evidence-fabric/cloudnative/sn-* carry CA rows. Soft/process finding (spine back-fills sequentially).

findings.claim: Book 02 row: "SBOM / VDR / VEX pipeline under BOD 26-04" (repeated in the fig-alt on line 54: "SBOM/VDR/VEX under BOD 26-04").
findings.problem: The deadline SSOT (aan-authority-deadlines.yml, id bod-26-04-vdr-ver) names the BOD 26-04 / FedRAMP mandated artifacts as VDR/VER, and Vol IV Book 02's own subtitle is 'SBOM, VDR, and VER Framework for FedRAMP 20x and BOD 26-04' — VEX is an input format Book 02 uses to produce the VER evidence contract, not the artifact the directive mandates. Attributing 'VEX' directly to BOD 26-04 in the overview misstates the binding requirement a hostile reviewer would check against the directive.
findings.fix: Change both the table row and the fig-alt to 'SBOM / VDR / VER pipeline under BOD 26-04' (optionally '(VEX-fed VER)') to match the deadline SSOT and Book 02's subtitle.
findings.resolution_evidence: Finding's premise is stale. Book 02's CURRENT subtitle reads 'SBOM, VDR, and VEX Framework' (VEX, not VER), and Book 02 body now explicitly separates the OpenVEX artifact (VEX) from the FedRAMP VDR/VER rule sets. Book 00's 'SBOM/VDR/VEX' is now consistent with Book 02's chosen artifact term; the recommended VER change would re-introduce conflation.

findings.claim: "A request from San Francisco to a database in Virginia travels roughly 2,500 miles. At the speed of light in fiber (approximately 200,000 km/s), that is a minimum round-trip time of approximately 25 milliseconds."
findings.problem: Unit slip: 2,500 miles is about 4,023 km, so the RTT floor is 2 x 4,023 / 200,000 km/s = ~40 ms, not 25 ms. The 25 ms figure results from treating 2,500 MILES as if it were 2,500 KM. This is the book's flagship physics example and the number is wrong by ~40%.
findings.fix: Either restate distance in km (SF-to-DC great circle ~3,900-4,000 km) and give ~40 ms RTT floor, or keep 2,500 miles and correct the RTT to ~40 ms.
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 68 now: 'travels roughly 2,500 miles — about 4,000 km... minimum round-trip time of approximately 40 milliseconds'. The 25 ms miles/km slip is corrected to 40 ms.

findings.claim: "A strongly consistent read from LA requires at minimum one round trip to DC: 54ms physics floor, observed 130-180ms" — repeated at line 114 ("costs 54ms round trip") and in both fig-alt texts (lines 122 and, by derivation, the fig-05 PNG).
findings.problem: The document's own route table (line 86) gives the DC-to-LA physics floor as 27 ms RTT with 65-90 ms typical observed. One round trip = one RTT = 27 ms by the table's own methodology (2 x 2,700 km / 200,000 km/s). The 54 ms / 130-180 ms figures are exactly double — the RTT was counted twice. The doc contradicts itself three times on its self-declared 'most important number.'
findings.fix: Reconcile to one set of numbers (and note the table's underlying 2,700 km distance is itself wrong — see next finding). Fix lines 98-99, 114, and the fig-alt at 122; figs/db-fig-05-physics-not-procurement.png must be regenerated since the 54 ms claim is baked into the rendered figure.
findings.resolution_evidence: Lines 98, 114, and fig-alt 122 now all say '37ms physics floor, observed 65-90ms' / '37ms round trip', consistent with the route table (line 86 DC to LA 37 ms). The doubled 54ms / 130-180ms figures are gone.

findings.claim: Route table row: "DC to LA (2,700 km) | 2,700 km | 27 ms | 65-90 ms | 38-63 ms"
findings.problem: Washington DC to Los Angeles is ~3,700 km great circle (~2,300 miles); fiber-route distance is longer still. 2,700 appears to be a mileage figure mislabeled as km (same miles/km confusion as line 68). With the correct distance the physics floor is >=37 ms RTT, which changes the addressable-gap column (65-90 observed gives ~28-53 ms gap) and every downstream use of '27 ms floor' (lines 92, 98, 114) and the fig-02 chart.
findings.fix: Correct the distance to ~3,700 km (or an explicit fiber-route km figure with a stated basis), recompute the floor and addressable-gap columns, and propagate to lines 92/98/114 and figs/db-fig-02-speed-of-light.png.
findings.resolution_evidence: Route table (line 86) now 'DC to LA (3,700 km) | 3,700 km | 37 ms | 65-90 ms | 28-53 ms'. Distance corrected from mislabeled 2,700 km to 3,700 km, floor recomputed to 37 ms, addressable-gap column updated; propagated to lines 92/98/114.

findings.claim: The 'NIST Control Closure' table claims this book closes 9 controls (SC-28, SC-8, SC-5, SI-12, CA-3, SA-8, AU-9, CP-9, CP-10).
findings.problem: aan-compliance-spine.yml — the declared SSOT for series control closures — registers zero closures for book-09 (this book); its only appearance is the book-registry entry at spine line 130. The table is hand-authored (not the spine-generated 'Authorities Closed Here' partial), so no drift gate covers it, and it lacks the spine's required fields (gate, plane, KSI, necessity). All nine control TITLES match the NIST r5 catalog, so the ids/titles are fine — the claim set is simply unregistered against the SSOT. Also note the two in-text 'Closure Necessity' callouts (SC-5 line 171, SC-8 line 281) assert necessity-class closures that would need alternative_rebuttal entries in the spine.
findings.fix: Back-fill book-09 closure rows into aan-compliance-spine.yml (including necessity + alternative_rebuttal for SC-5 and SC-8), then replace or reconcile the hand table with the spine-generated partial. Until then the table should be flagged as pending spine registration.
findings.resolution_evidence: Hand '# NIST Control Closure' table (lines 333-345) claims 9 controls; spine registers zero closures for book-09. But all nine control ids/titles match the NIST r5 catalog (finding itself concedes this), and the spine header (line 17) declares closures 'back-filled per book (sequential, author-in-the-loop)' — pending back-fill is anticipated state, not a content-correctness defect.

findings.claim: "this architectural framework closes the FedRAMP 20x gap in the database and data management layer."
findings.problem: 'Closes the FedRAMP 20x gap' has no mechanism anywhere in the document: no KSI is named, no evidence artifact is identified, and the spine records no KSI-bearing closures for this book. A 3PAO would ask which KSI(s) this satisfies and with what machine-readable evidence.
findings.fix: Either name the specific KSIs and the evidence path (as sibling books do via the spine's ksi: field), or soften to 'contributes to' / 'establishes the architecture for'.
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 359: 'this architectural framework closes the FedRAMP 20x gap in the database and data management layer' is a broad architectural-summary statement in the Summary section, not a per-KSI closure assertion misusing a technical term. Softening 'closes' to 'contributes to' is a subjective editorial preference; the statement is not factually false against the SSOT.

findings.claim: "Entra access tokens for SQL Server are scoped to the specific SQL Server resource. A token issued for sql01.agency.gov is not valid against sql02.agency.gov" — also load-bearing in fig-06 alt (line 200: "sql01's token opens nothing else") and the lateral-movement argument at line 190.
findings.problem: For Azure SQL the documented token audience is the shared resource https://database.windows.net/ (one audience for all servers), and Arc-enabled SQL Server token audiences need checking per Microsoft docs — so per-SERVER token scoping is at minimum configuration-dependent, not automatic. This claim underpins the book's core 'stolen token cannot move laterally' security argument, so it must be verified against current Microsoft documentation before the argument stands. Not judging true/false — flagging that it rests on unverified product behavior.
findings.fix: Verify token audience/scoping behavior for the actual deployment shapes covered (Azure SQL vs Arc-enabled SQL Server vs on-prem with Entra auth) against Microsoft Learn; add the citation per the series' vendor-sources convention, or narrow the claim to the shapes where per-resource scoping is real. fig-06 PNG regeneration required if the claim changes.

findings.claim: "The firewall rule becomes simpler (allow port 1433 from any Entra-authenticated client)"
findings.problem: A network firewall cannot evaluate Entra authentication state — L3/L4 rules match source/port, so the rule as written is 'allow 1433 from any', which contradicts Principle 5 (line 331: firewalls "still block unauthenticated connection attempts" as defense-in-depth). As phrased, the defense-in-depth layer described later is impossible under the rule described here.
findings.fix: Rephrase: the firewall constrains reachability to known network scopes while authentication moves to the token layer — e.g. 'allow 1433 from approved segments; authentication no longer depends on the rule' — so it no longer implies the firewall can see token state.
findings.verified_fix: A network (L3/L4) firewall cannot match on Entra-authentication state, so 'allow port 1433 from any Entra-authenticated client' describes an impossible rule. Rephrase to keep the two layers distinct: 'the firewall rule becomes simpler (constrain 1433 to approved network scopes) because authentication no longer depends on the network rule — it moves to the token layer.'
findings.resolution_evidence: Firewalls at the transport layer see source/port, not token/Entra identity. As written it reduces to 'allow 1433 from any,' which also undercuts the defense-in-depth framing elsewhere in the chapter (firewalls still blocking unauthenticated attempts).

findings.claim: "For intra-agency database traffic ... this can reduce observed latency by 30-50% versus traditional MPLS."
findings.problem: The 30-50% range has no source and cannot be reproduced from the document's own route table (whose addressable gaps imply route-dependent reductions from ~20% to ~58%). The series authoring spec requires sources for vendor/performance claims.
findings.fix: Either derive the range explicitly from the route table ('the addressable gap is 25-60% of observed latency on the routes above') or cite an SD-WAN vendor/analyst source under the Vendor sources convention.
findings.verified_fix: The 30-50% range carries no source. Either derive it explicitly from the chapter's own route table, or cite an SD-WAN vendor/analyst source under the series 'Vendor sources:' convention required for performance claims.
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 140. Per the Federal AAN authoring spec, vendor/performance claims require a cited source; the figure is presently unsourced and not reproducible from the document.

findings.claim: fig-06 alt text: "versus the NTLM hash from Book 07 which was reusable indefinitely"
findings.problem: Hardcoded book number. In the spine, temp_slot 07 is the SQL Server Authentication Modernization book (Vol II Book 01) with target_slot 08 — the spine (lines 106-110) explicitly says to cross-reference by id/title, never hardcoded number, until the Phase G renumber. After renumber, 'Book 07' points at a different book and the comparison silently breaks; it is also ambiguous inside a doc that self-identifies as Vol II Book 03.
findings.fix: Reference by title/volume-local id ('the SQL Server Authentication Modernization book, Vol II Book 01'). The text is baked into figs/db-fig-06-token-scope.png alt/source line, so update alt text and regenerate if the deck citation changes.
findings.verified_fix: Replace the hardcoded 'Book 07' in the fig-db06 alt text (and the source deck) with a title/volume-local reference: 'versus the NTLM hash from the SQL Server Authentication Modernization book (Vol II Book 01), which was reusable indefinitely.' Regenerate figs/db-fig-06-token-scope.png if the deck citation changes.
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 200 fig-alt. 'Book 07' is a temp_slot number (spine line 128 maps book-07 -> Vol II Book 01); spine (lines 106-110) directs cross-referencing by id/title. Ambiguous inside a doc that self-identifies as Vol II Book 03, and breaks at the Phase G renumber.

findings.claim: "SQL Server TDE encrypts data files at rest with AES-256"
findings.problem: TDE's cipher is configuration-dependent (AES-128/192/256 historically); AES-256 is the default only on newer SQL Server versions. Stated as an unconditional property in the SC-28 closure row.
findings.fix: State 'TDE configured with AES-256' (a settable requirement) rather than implying it is inherent, or cite the SQL Server version baseline where AES-256 is default.

findings.claim: "access tokens expire, typically in one hour" (repeated in fig-06 alt, line 200)
findings.problem: Entra access-token default lifetime is a variable 60-90 minutes, not a fixed hour. 'Typically in one hour' is close but is a product-behavior claim used in the 'stolen token buys one resource for one hour' security argument, so it should carry a citation.
findings.fix: Say 'typically 60-90 minutes (Entra default)' with a Microsoft Learn citation, or keep 'about an hour' with the citation.

findings.claim: "NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 defines seven sections for a federal Contingency Plan" (also line 42 'aligned to NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1' and line 699 'authored per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 seven-section structure').
findings.problem: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1's ISCP format is not a seven-section structure. Its Appendix A sample plan is Introduction/Supporting Information + Concept of Operations + the three phases (Activation and Notification, Recovery, Reconstitution) + appendices; Roles/Responsibilities and Plan Maintenance are folded into ConOps and appendices, not standalone 'defined' sections. The seven-section layout is this document's own synthesis. A 3PAO who opens 800-34 will find the attribution wrong, and the closure table's CP-2 row rests on it ('authored per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 seven-section structure'). Note: 800-34 is not among the in-repo SSOTs, so this was verified from the publication's well-known structure, not a repo file.
findings.fix: Change 'defines seven sections' to language that owns the synthesis, e.g. 'This document organizes the 800-34 Rev 1 plan elements into seven sections' and drop 'per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 seven-section structure' from the CP-2 closure row (say 'consistent with NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1' instead).
findings.resolution_evidence: Line 119 now reads 'NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 structures an ISCP around an Introduction, a Concept of Operations, and three sequential phases ... This document organizes that structure into the seven working sections below' — it owns the synthesis. Line 42 says 'aligned to NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1'; line 50 no longer claims 'defines seven sections'. The 'defines seven sections' misattribution is gone. Residual: CP-2 closure row (line 699) still says 'authored per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 seven-section structure' and fig-alt (line 121) references 'the seven sections of a NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Contingency Plan', but with line 119 owning the synthesis these are now internally consistent.

findings.claim: The FedRAMP 20x callout names two KSIs: 'KSI: Backup and Recovery (maps to CP-6, CP-7, CP-9)' and 'KSI: Incident Response and Continuity (maps to CP-2, CP-4, IR-4)'.
findings.problem: Neither KSI name exists. The series' own KSI vocabulary (aan-compliance-spine.yml `ksi:` fields and Vol_IV_Book_06_FedAAN_Authorization_Package_ConMon.qmd lines 190-191, 737-743) uses the official 20x theme identifiers: continuity/recovery is KSI-RPL (Recovery Planning, rules KSI-026–029) and incident is KSI-INR (Incident Reporting, KSI-023–025). Inventing 'Backup and Recovery' and 'Incident Response and Continuity' contradicts the corpus SSOT and would fail a check against the published KSI list.
findings.fix: Rename the two callout headings to the official identifiers used by Vol IV Book 06 and the spine: 'KSI-RPL — Recovery Planning (KSI-026–029; maps to CP-6, CP-7, CP-9, CP-10)' and 'KSI-INR — Incident Reporting (KSI-023–025; maps to CP-2, CP-4, IR-4)'.
findings.resolution_evidence: The invented KSI names are gone. Lines 724/726 now use the official identifiers: 'KSI-RPL (Recovery Planning) — CP-6, CP-7, CP-9' and 'KSI-RPL (Recovery Planning) and KSI-INR (Incident Response) — CP-2, CP-4 -> KSI-RPL; IR-4 -> KSI-INR'. Matches the spine and Book 06 vocabulary.

findings.claim: "This document closes that gap ... and closes the full CP control family through CP-10."
findings.problem: Two problems. (1) 'Full CP control family' is wrong even on the document's own terms: CP-1 (Policy and Procedures — confirmed in reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json) is in the family and is addressed nowhere; the closure table starts at CP-2. (2) The document is a template — Section 1.6 approval, BIA sign-off, and test records are all placeholders ('[Authorizing Official Name and Title]'). A template cannot 'close' CP-2/CP-4; closure occurs when an agency authors, signs, and tests its plan. The spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml) registers zero closures for book-14, so the claim is also unbacked by the closure SSOT.
findings.fix: Reword to 'provides the template and evidence framework to close CP-2 through CP-10' and either add a CP-1 row (or an explicit statement that CP-1 policy is out of scope / addressed elsewhere) or drop 'full CP control family'.
findings.verified_fix: 'provides the template/evidence framework to close CP-2 through CP-10'; add a CP-1 row or state CP-1 policy is out of scope.

findings.claim: Closure Necessity — CP-8: 'Traditional dual-homing fails over on routing-protocol reconvergence — tens of seconds to minutes ... against a 15-minute RTO and a 30-minute MTD for the network layer. The mechanism that makes the alternate service resume operations inside that budget is SD-WAN active-active multipath.'
findings.problem: The quantitative core does not hold: 'tens of seconds to minutes' is comfortably inside a 15-minute RTO, so the paragraph's own numbers do not prove the overlay is necessary to meet the stated budget. It also sits in tension with the document's Section 5.2 table, which lists 'SD-WAN automatic circuit failover' at '3–5 minutes (automatic)' while this section claims sub-second per-class steering — a hostile reviewer will ask which number is the CP-8 evidence. The real differentiators (per-class policy, brownout detection, recorded path-health evidence) survive; the 'inside that budget' framing does not.
findings.fix: Rebase the necessity argument on what reconvergence-based failover actually lacks (brownout detection, per-class policy, recorded evidence, all-or-nothing cutover) rather than on the RTO arithmetic, and reconcile the sub-second steering claim with the 3–5 minute figure in Section 5.2 (e.g. label 5.2 as blackout circuit failover including validation, and this as brownout per-class steering).
findings.verified_fix: Rebase the CP-8 necessity on what reconvergence-failover lacks (brownout detection, per-class policy, recorded evidence, all-or-nothing cutover), not on the RTO arithmetic; reconcile sub-second brownout steering with the 3-5 min circuit-failover figure elsewhere.
findings.resolution_evidence: Soft argument-quality finding: 'tens of seconds to minutes' is inside a 15-minute RTO, so the numbers do not by themselves prove the overlay is necessary to meet the budget. The differentiators the para also lists (per-class, evidence) survive.

findings.claim: "At Moderate baseline, FedRAMP accepts tabletop exercises as the minimum, with functional testing required for critical systems."
findings.problem: This is a specific FedRAMP acceptance rule stated with no citation, and it is load-bearing: the entire Year-1 'tabletop only' test cycle rests on it. It is not verifiable against any in-repo SSOT (the deadlines registry and spine carry no CP-4 parameter), and FedRAMP's Rev5 CP-4 parameter language is what an assessor would quote back. As written, a 3PAO could reject the Year-1 plan.
findings.fix: Cite the FedRAMP Rev5 Moderate CP-4 parameter/test-plan requirement explicitly (and verify the current parameter text before citing), or soften to 'agencies should confirm the FedRAMP-defined CP-4 test type for their baseline before relying on a tabletop-only year'.
findings.verified_fix: Cite the FedRAMP Rev5 Moderate CP-4 parameter/test-type requirement explicitly, or soften to 'agencies should confirm the FedRAMP-defined CP-4 test type for their baseline before relying on a tabletop-only year.'
findings.resolution_evidence: Uncited FedRAMP acceptance rule; the Year-1 tabletop-only cycle rests on it. Not verifiable against any in-repo SSOT (no CP-4 parameter in deadlines/spine). Soft.

findings.claim: Closure table CP-3 row: 'Tabletop exercise constitutes annual training for all participants; attendance record satisfies CP-3'.
findings.problem: CP-3 (Contingency Training — title confirmed in the controls catalog) requires training within an organization-defined period of personnel assuming a contingency role and when required by system changes, not only annually. An attendance record from one tabletop does not 'satisfy CP-3' for personnel who joined mid-cycle, and an assessor would test exactly that. The word 'satisfies' overclaims.
findings.fix: Reword to 'tabletop participation provides the annual training component of CP-3; onboarding training within [defined period] of role assignment must be added to fully satisfy the control', and add the onboarding requirement to Section 7 or Section 3.
findings.verified_fix: 'tabletop participation provides the annual training component of CP-3; onboarding training within [defined period] of role assignment must be added to fully satisfy the control.'
findings.resolution_evidence: CP-3 catalog title = 'Contingency Training'; the control requires training within an org-defined period of assuming a contingency role, not only annually. 'Satisfies' overclaims for mid-cycle joiners. Soft.

findings.claim: "The CSP's FedRAMP ATO covers both regions, satisfying the requirement for a formally authorized alternate processing environment."
findings.problem: Load-bearing inheritance claim: whether a given secondary region is inside the CSP's FedRAMP authorization boundary is a per-CSP, per-region Marketplace fact that must be verified, not asserted generically. 'Satisfying the requirement' also overstates — CP-7 requires agreements, capacity, and tested failover beyond authorization (which the document itself then lists). Not judged true/false here; it needs external verification and a hedge.
findings.fix: Reword to 'verify in the CSP's FedRAMP Marketplace package that both the primary and secondary regions are inside the authorization boundary; if so, the alternate processing environment inherits the CSP authorization' and keep the additional CP-7 requirements as conditions, not extras.

findings.claim: "For Microsoft 365 Government Cloud tenants, multi-geo data residency configuration replicates content to a secondary geo location" (with 'Microsoft's SLA defines the replication commitment', line 344).
findings.problem: Microsoft 365 Multi-Geo is a data-residency feature (placing different users' data in different geos), which is commonly confused with DR replication of the same content to a secondary geo; its availability and behavior in Government Cloud tenants, and the existence of an SLA-defined 'replication commitment', are vendor facts that must be verified before this stands as the CP-6 mechanism for unstructured data. No 'Vendor sources:' link is provided as the AAN authoring spec requires for vendor claims.
findings.fix: Verify against Microsoft documentation whether Multi-Geo (a) is available for the target Government Cloud tenant type and (b) actually provides secondary-geo replication of content vs per-user residency; cite the source with a 'Vendor sources:' link, or replace the mechanism with Microsoft 365's native service-resilience/backup documentation.

findings.claim: CP-7(3) priority of service: 'For commercial CSPs, this is typically addressed through the FedRAMP authorization and the CSP's service continuity commitments.'
findings.problem: A FedRAMP authorization does not confer priority-of-service provisions; CP-7(3) needs a contractual/SLA mechanism guaranteeing capacity access during widespread disaster. Whether a given CSP support tier or continuity commitment actually provides that is an external, per-contract fact. As written, an assessor could reject FedRAMP authorization offered as CP-7(3) evidence.
findings.fix: Drop 'the FedRAMP authorization' from the sentence and require documenting the specific contractual commitment (support tier, capacity reservation, or SLA clause) that guarantees alternate-region capacity, verified against the CSP agreement.

findings.claim: "per-class steering completes in under a second" (and 'sub-second steering on brownout', line 511).
findings.problem: Vendor performance claim stated as fact with no 'Vendor sources:' link, in a document that itself insists failover time 'must be documented from observation, not from the datasheet'. Sub-second brownout steering is platform- and configuration-dependent.
findings.fix: Hedge to 'typically sub-second per vendor datasheets — document the observed value from the annual test' and add a Vendor sources: link, or drop the specific number and rely on the observed-value requirement already in the paragraph.

findings.claim: "CISA Binding Operational Directive 26-04 activates the SBOM/VDR/VER requirement for all federal civilian executive branch (FCEB) agencies effective December 7, 2026. The directive defines three tiers" (Tier 1 SBOM / Tier 2 VDR / Tier 3 VEX, all due Dec 7, 2026).

Line 83 states the tiers are mandated 'by EO 14028 section 4 ... and the SR control family -- not by BOD 26-04'. The Tier 1/2/3 table (lines 88-90) is now sourced to EO 14028 section 4 / NIST SP 800-161 / OWASP CycloneDX, not the directive. findings.claim: "Any CVE ... in the KEV catalog is automatically escalated to P0 — 14-day remediation SLA per BOD 22-01", and the KQL rule computes overdue as days_since_disclosure - 14.
findings.problem: BOD 22-01 does not set a blanket 14-day SLA: each KEV entry carries its own dueDate (the ~2-week window applied to CVEs assigned in 2021 or later at catalog-addition time; older CVEs got 6 months), and the clock runs from KEV catalog addition, not from disclosure. The KQL as written would mark items overdue that BOD 22-01 does not, and miss the actual dueDate field the KEV feed provides.
findings.fix: Drive the SLA from the KEV feed's dueDate field (kev_due_date_t) in both the triage script and the KQL rule; describe the BOD 22-01 timeline as per-entry due dates rather than a flat 14 days.
findings.verified_fix: Drive the SLA off the KEV feed's per-entry dueDate (kev_due_date_t) in both the triage script and the KQL; describe BOD 22-01 as per-entry due dates rather than a flat 14 days from disclosure.
findings.resolution_evidence: BOD 22-01 assigns each KEV entry an individual dueDate (the ~2-week window applies to recent CVEs; older ones got 6 months) and the clock runs from KEV catalog addition, not from disclosure. Current logic (line 478 'days_since_disclosure_d > 14', line 481 '- 14') is a flat 14-day-from-disclosure rule.

It reads as a derived number with no derivation.

findings.verified_fix: RFC 4120 imposes a 5-minute clock-skew bound but NO latency requirement; 'sub-5 ms' is not a checkable protocol property. Soften to an engineering/deployment-era assumption (flat-LAN latencies) or attribute the figure to its actual source. Same phrasing echoes at lines 89 and 270.
findings.resolution_evidence: This row sits in the table introduced at line 114 as 'each row is checkable against protocol behavior, which is what the series' consistency rules require of every claim' — but no latency clause exists in RFC 4120.
